passages: It lies northeast of [Big Bend National Park](https://national-parks.org/united-states/big-bend/) and south of [Carlsbad Caverns National Park](https://national-parks.org/united-states/carlsbad-caverns/).
The park preserves the rugged Guadalupe Mountains, which contain the four highest peaks in Texas, including the state’s highest point, Guadalupe Peak.

Known for its dramatic desert scenery, fossil-rich geology, and diverse ecosystems, Guadalupe Mountains National Park offers visitors one of the finest wilderness experiences in the southern United States.
Guadalupe Mountains National Park is best known for its towering peaks, spectacular canyons, and extensive hiking opportunities.
Visitors are drawn to the challenge of climbing Guadalupe Peak, which rises to 8,751 feet (2,667 meters) above sea level and offers panoramic views across Texas and New Mexico.
The park is also famous for the stunning beauty of McKittrick Canyon, where colorful autumn foliage creates one of the most remarkable fall displays in Texas.
### Guadalupe Peak
Guadalupe Peak is also affectionately known as Signal Peak and it reaches a summit of 8,751 feet (2,667 m).
This represents the tallest point in Texas.
### El Capitan
![](https://national-parks.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Guadalupe20Mountains.jpg)El Capitan is a stunning peak located here in the Guadalupe Mountains.
It is an iconic picturesque mountain that appears more like a thrown sitting atop of an eroded mountain.
It reaches a summit of 8,085 feet (2,464 m) and is the 10th tallest mountain in Texas.
It is a symbol of the Texas west, but it is not to be mistaken for the more famous El Capitan in [Yosemite National Park](https://national-parks.org/united-states/yosemite).
### Tallest Point in Texas
Guadalupe Peak, standing at an impressive 8,749 feet (2,667 meters) above sea level, is the highest point in Texas and a prominent feature of Guadalupe Mountains National Park.
This iconic peak offers a challenging yet rewarding hiking experience, attracting outdoor enthusiasts and adventurers from far and wide.
The trail to Guadalupe Peak winds through rugged terrain, ascending over 3,000 feet (914 meters) in elevation gain along a well-marked path.
Hikers are treated to breathtaking panoramic views of the surrounding desert landscape as they climb higher, with glimpses of distant mountain ranges and expansive vistas stretching to the horizon.
There are also climbing opportunities as well.
![Guadalupe Peak Trail Guadalupe Mountains National Park](https://national-parks.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Guadalupe-Peak-Trail-Guadalupe-Mountains-National-Park-1024x576.png)
### Guadalupe Peak Trail
**Distance:** 8.5 miles (13.7 km) round trip
**Elevation Gain:** Approximately 3,000 feet (914 m)
**Description:**
Guadalupe Peak Trail leads to the highest point in Texas at 8,751 feet, making it the signature hike of Guadalupe Mountains National Park.
The well-maintained trail climbs steadily through fragrant pine forests, rugged limestone slopes, and exposed ridgelines before reaching the famous summit pyramid monument.
### Devil's Hall Trail
**Distance:** 4.2 miles (6.8 km) round trip
**Elevation Gain:** Approximately 550 feet (168 m)
**Rating:** Moderate
**Description:**
Devil’s Hall Trail is one of the park’s most unique hikes, leading through the rocky wash of Pine Spring Canyon before entering a dramatic natural corridor known as Devil’s Hall.
### McKittrick Canyon Trail
**Distance:** 6.8 miles (10.9 km) round trip *(to Pratt Cabin)*
**Elevation Gain:** Approximately 700 feet (213 m)
**Rating:** Moderate
**Description:**
McKittrick Canyon Trail showcases a surprisingly lush oasis hidden within the rugged Guadalupe Mountains.

Guadalupe Mountains National Park, located in west Texas, is known for its rugged beauty, towering peaks, and extensive network of hiking trails.
The park is home to Guadalupe Peak, the highest point in Texas, reaching an elevation of 8,749 feet (2,667 meters).
It is also known for its stunning desert landscapes, including deep canyons, colorful rock formations, and ancient fossilized reefs.
You visit Guadalupe Mountains National Park to experience some of the most spectacular mountain scenery in Texas.

The park is home to **Guadalupe Peak**, the highest point in Texas at **8,751 feet**, along with dramatic limestone cliffs, deep canyons, pristine desert landscapes, colorful wildflowers, and one of the world’s finest fossil reef systems.
Located in far western Texas near the New Mexico border, the park preserves a portion of the ancient Capitan Reef, which formed beneath a tropical sea approximately 265 million years ago.

passages: # Guadalupe Peak’s Reign as Tallest Mountain in Texas

![](https://i0.wp.com/mountainfieldguide.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Guadalupe-peak-Texas.-Beautiful-mountain-peak-in-the-back-ground-with-a-blue-grey-sky-Desert-in-the-fore-ground-with-cactus-and-a-pointy-hill-side.jpg?resize=750%2C500&ssl=1)
Rising dramatically above the Chihuahuan Desert, Guadalupe Peak holds an undisputed place in Texas geography.
Its summit reaches 8,751 feet above sea level, making it the highest natural point—and tallest recognized mountain summit—in the Lone Star State.

Located within Guadalupe Mountains National Park, the peak combines sweeping desert views, remarkably preserved marine fossils, high-elevation forests, and one of the most rewarding summit hikes in the American Southwest.

Guadalupe Peak is the highest summit in the [Guadalupe Mountains](https://mountainfieldguide.com/road-trip-to-carlsbad-caverns-and-the-guadalupe-mountains/), a rugged range extending across western Texas and southeastern New Mexico.
Although the mountain rises from an arid desert landscape, its upper slopes contain pockets of pine and fir forest.
The climb from Pine Springs passes through several ecological zones before reaching an exposed summit overlooking El Capitan, the Salt Basin, and distant mountain ranges.
Guadalupe Peak is also one of the United States’ official state high points.
It attracts hikers, peak baggers, geologists, wildlife enthusiasts, and travelers exploring Guadalupe Mountains National Park and nearby Carlsbad Caverns National Park.
The mountain’s elevation is impressive by Texas standards, but its true distinction lies in its relief.
Guadalupe Peak rises more than 3,000 feet above the surrounding landscape, appearing like a massive limestone fortress above the desert.
## ⚡ Fast Facts
| **Country** | United States |
| **State/Province** | Texas |
| **County/Region** | Culberson County |
It stands within Guadalupe Mountains National Park, approximately three miles west of the Pine Springs area.
The mountain is part of a prominent limestone escarpment that rises abruptly from the Chihuahuan Desert.
El Capitan, one of the park’s most recognizable landmarks, stands immediately southeast of Guadalupe Peak.
Fuel, food, lodging, and other supplies should be arranged before entering the park.
![](https://i0.wp.com/mountainfieldguide.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Guadalupe-Peak-Trail-Guadalupe-Mountains-National-Park-Texas.jpg?resize=750%2C595&ssl=1)
## 📏 Elevation & Prominence
The National Park Service lists Guadalupe Peak’s elevation as **8,751 feet**, establishing it as the highest natural point in Texas.
Modern lidar measurements place the summit at approximately 8,749.9 feet.
The small difference reflects changes in surveying methods, elevation datums, and rounding rather than a meaningful disagreement about the mountain’s status.
It is not merely a high point on a broad plateau; it is an independently commanding mountain with significant vertical relief.
Its topographic isolation is approximately 72.64 miles, meaning hikers must travel that far before reaching terrain that rises higher.
Peakbagger identifies Sacramento Lookout in New Mexico as its nearest higher neighbor, while Sierra Blanca Peak is listed as its line parent.
However, none rise as high above sea level as Guadalupe Peak.
The Guadalupe Mountains contain most of the state’s highest summits.
Bush Mountain, Shumard Peak, Bartlett Peak, Hunter Peak, and El Capitan all reach impressive elevations, but each remains below Guadalupe Peak.
Guadalupe Peak may not be among the highest mountains in the United States, but within Texas it occupies an unmistakable throne.

![](https://i0.wp.com/mountainfieldguide.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Thickets-of-cacti-Opuntia-sp.-among-dry-desert-vegetation-in-Guadalupe-Mountains-National-Park-Texas-USA.jpg?resize=750%2C457&ssl=1)
## 🪨 Geology
Learn more about the broader processes behind mountain uplift in [How Are Mountains Formed?](https://mountainfieldguide.com/how-are-mountains-formed/).
![](https://i0.wp.com/mountainfieldguide.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Female-Great-tailed-Grackle-in-a-Texas-Madrone-tree-in-Guadalupe-Mountains-National-Park.jpg?resize=750%2C500&ssl=1)
## 🌿 Flora & Fauna
Guadalupe Peak rises through several ecological zones, creating a surprising variety of plant and animal habitats.
### Chihuahuan Desert
American Airlines installed the monument in 1958 to commemorate the 100th anniversary of the Butterfield Overland Mail route, which passed south of the mountain.
The monument has become one of the most recognizable state-highpoint markers in the United States.
From the summit, hikers can look south toward El Capitan, west across the Salt Basin, and north toward the higher interior of the Guadalupe Mountains.
## 🌤️ Best Time to Visit
### El Capitan
El Capitan rises immediately southeast of Guadalupe Peak and forms one of the most recognizable mountain profiles in Texas.
Its sheer limestone face was an important landmark for Indigenous peoples, explorers, surveyors, stagecoach travelers, and settlers crossing the surrounding desert.
There is no maintained trail to its summit, but excellent views are available from Highway 62/180 and the Guadalupe Peak Trail.
### McKittrick Canyon
Its caves formed within the same broad Guadalupe Mountains geological system.
Combining the two parks creates an excellent road trip through desert mountains, fossil reefs, caves, and historic landscapes.
Read about a firsthand visit in [Road Trip to Carlsbad Caverns and the Guadalupe Mountains](https://mountainfieldguide.com/road-trip-to-carlsbad-caverns-and-the-guadalupe-mountains/).
## 💡 Fun Facts
The National Park Service uses an elevation of 8,751 feet.
Modern lidar data measures the summit at approximately 8,749.9 feet.
The difference is caused by surveying methods, elevation datums, and rounding.
Yes.
### Is there water on the Guadalupe Peak Trail?
No reliable drinking water is available along the trail.
Hikers must carry all the water they expect to need.
Yes.

# Guadalupe Peak: The Highest Point in Texas
Guadalupe Peak, also known as Signal Peak, is the highest point in Texas.
It is in [Guadalupe Mountains National Park](/handbook/entries/guadalupe-mountains-national-park) three miles west of Pine Springs in northwestern Culberson County (at 31°53' N, 104°52' W).
Its summit, with an elevation of 8,749 feet above sea level, rises 3,100 feet above Pine Springs.

The peak towers over nearby Guadalupe Pass, and nineteenth-century travelers, including [John Russell Bartlett](/handbook/entries/bartlett-john-russell), were often deceived by the peak's great height and the clear mountain air; they reported seeing the peak a full week before they reached it and consistently underestimated their distance from it.

passages: # The Ultimate Guide to Hiking Guadalupe Peak: Trail Guide, Preparation, and the Two Guadalupes of Texas
For outdoor enthusiasts, the name "Guadalupe" represents two of the state's most iconic, yet fundamentally different, natural wonders.
On one hand, it refers to the highest summit in the Lone Star State: Guadalupe Peak, located in the remote high-desert mountains of West Texas.
On the other hand, it signifies the Guadalupe River: a cypress-shaded, cool-water paradise winding through the heart of the Central Texas Hill Country.
For hikers, backpackers, and families planning their next great outdoor escape in 2026, understanding what each destination demands — and offers — is the key to a successful trip.

This guide provides a comprehensive trail-by-trail breakdown of the grueling ascent to the "Top of Texas" at Guadalupe Peak, details the essential preparations required to survive the high-altitude desert, and helps you navigate the massive geographical divide between the rugged peaks of West Texas and the refreshing waters of Central Texas.
## Conquering the Top of Texas: An Overview of Guadalupe Peak
Rising high above the surrounding Chihuahuan Desert, Guadalupe Peak stands as the highest point in Texas at an elevation of 8,751 feet.

Located within Guadalupe Mountains National Park in remote Culberson County — roughly 110 miles east of El Paso and near the small community of Salt Flat — this imposing limestone peak is a bucket-list destination for hikers from around the world.
Check current conditions on the official [National Park Service trail page](https://www.nps.gov/thingstodo/gumo_hike_guadalupe_peak.htm) before you go.
## The Trail Breakdown: An 8.4-Mile Ascent to the Summit
The journey to the summit is a classic out-and-back trail.
### The Trailhead: Starting at Pine Springs
The hike begins at the Pine Springs Trailhead, located next to the Pine Springs Campground at an elevation of approximately 5,829 feet.
Here, visitors must register at the self-pay kiosk or display their national park pass before setting out.
The ground is dominated by loose limestone gravel and uneven rock steps, requiring constant focus on foot placement.
In this initial stretch, you will gain over 1,200 feet of elevation.
The key to surviving this portion of the trail is pacing.
| **Trail Type** | Out-and-back |
| **Total Round-Trip Distance** | 8.4 miles |
| **Starting Elevation** | 5,829 feet (Pine Springs Trailhead) |

### 1. Water Requirements: The Golden Rule
There is absolutely no water available on the trail or at the summit.
The air is extremely dry, and the physical exertion is high.
## A Tale of Two Guadalupes: West Texas Peaks vs. Central Texas Rivers
A common point of confusion for out-of-state visitors — and even some native Texans — is the geographic distinction surrounding the name "Guadalupe" in Texas.
It is crucial to understand that Guadalupe Mountains National Park and the Guadalupe River are located in entirely different regions of the state, separated by nearly 450 miles of highway.

# Hiking Guadalupe Peak in 2026: Your Complete Guide to Texas' Highest Point, Plus a River Recovery Day
![Hikers on the Guadalupe Peak Trail with El Capitan in the background, Guadalupe Mountains National Park, West Texas](/assets/tubing-canyon-view-Cznh8hcT.jpg)
## Introduction: Conquering the Top of Texas

Standing at 8,751 feet above sea level in the far western corner of the Lone Star State, Guadalupe Peak is the highest point in Texas — and one of the most rewarding day hikes in the American Southwest.
Located inside Guadalupe Mountains National Park, roughly 110 miles east of El Paso and 90 miles west of Carlsbad, New Mexico, this is genuinely remote, rugged West Texas terrain.

This guide covers everything a hiker or trip planner needs to know before attempting Guadalupe Peak in 2026: exact trail statistics, a step-by-step route breakdown, seasonal weather strategies, a gear and water checklist, permit and fee logistics, family and pet policies, and campsite options.

It also clarifies one of the most common points of confusion for Texas travelers — the difference between Guadalupe Peak in West Texas, the Guadalupe River in the Hill Country, and Guadalupe River State Park — and offers a practical 3–4 day Texas itinerary for those who want to [pair the summit experience](/cabanas) with a [restful recovery day on the water](/blog/tubing-guadalupe-river-new-braunfels).
Whether you're an experienced hiker ticking off state highpoints or a family planning your first serious mountain day, this guide will help you show up prepared and finish safely.

### The Final Push to the Summit (and Stainless Steel Pyramid)
![Stainless steel pyramid summit monument at Guadalupe Peak, 8,751 feet, Texas' highest point](/assets/aerial-cabanas-B9gWMsj2.jpg)
The last mile to the summit is the most technically demanding stretch.
The trail steepens again, navigating rock outcroppings and loose scree before arriving at a stainless steel pyramid monument marking the summit at 8,751 feet.
The monument was placed by American Airlines to commemorate early airmail routes — a surprisingly moving detail at an otherwise ancient geological landmark.
Some hikers also find Weather Underground and Windy.com helpful for hourly ridge-level wind modeling.
If the forecast shows sustained gusts above 40 mph at 8,000 feet, consider postponing or choosing an alternative park activity.
Hiking in extreme wind is exhausting, potentially dangerous, and removes most of the summit experience anyway.

### Navigation and Safety Gear

**Leave No Trace note:** The Guadalupe Peak Trail is a pack-in, pack-out environment. There are no trash cans on the trail. Human waste must be managed with a WAG bag (available at the visitor center) if you need to go anywhere beyond established restrooms. Do not bury waste on this trail — soil depth and decomposition rates in the desert environment cannot handle the impact.
### Footwear, Trekking Poles, and Traction Considerations
Guadalupe Mountains National Park charges a **$15 per-person entrance fee** (ages 16 and up), valid for 7 consecutive days.

The **America the Beautiful Annual Pass** ($80 for the year) covers entrance for the pass holder and passengers in a personal vehicle and is excellent value if you plan to visit multiple national parks or monuments in 2026.
The pass is available at the Pine Springs Visitor Center or online at [store.usgs.gov](https://store.usgs.gov).

If you arrive late and the lot is full, there is limited legal roadside parking on the highway frontage, but it is not ideal. **Arrive by 6:30–7:00 a.m. at the absolute latest during peak season.** Starting before full sunrise also positions you to beat both the heat and the wind, which typically build through the morning.
There is no food available at the trailhead or visitor center.
The nearest fuel and food is roughly 35 miles west in Dell City or 55 miles east in Whites City/Carlsbad.
**Day hikers** do not need a backcountry permit — the park entrance fee is sufficient.

**Overnight hikers** who wish to camp at the **Guadalupe Peak Backcountry Campground** (approximately 0.5 miles from the summit) must obtain a free backcountry permit. Permits are self-issued at the Pine Springs Visitor Center and are available on a first-come, first-served basis. Capacity at the backcountry sites is limited, and popular weekends can see the permit board fill early. There are no campfires permitted anywhere in the park's backcountry, and food must be stored in bear-resistant containers or hung at least 200 feet from your campsite to deter mule deer, ringtail cats, and other wildlife.

**Pine Springs Campground** (near the visitor center) offers tent and RV sites with restrooms, water, and some electrical hookups. Reservations are made via [recreation.gov](https://www.recreation.gov) and are strongly recommended for fall weekends and holidays. Dog Creek and other frontcountry sites are available in the park as well.
Restrooms with flush toilets are available at the Pine Springs Visitor Center.
There are no restroom facilities on the trail itself.
Parking is on-site.
Restrooms and showers are available — a meaningful detail when your hiking gear still smells like two days of West Texas trail.
The [shuttle-assisted tubing](/tubing) float handles the river logistics (no separate car shuffle, no walking a long distance back to your vehicle), and the float ends back at your private cabana.
